title: The Cost of One Meal
paragraphs:
The Cost of One Meal
Esau’s Story — Genesis 25:29–34
He traded his future for a full stomach.

One meal.
One craving.
One reckless moment.

Esau came in from the field exhausted, hungry, desperate. Jacob had stew. Esau had appetite. And in that moment, appetite became his master. He said, “I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?” So he sold what was sacred for something that would disappear by nightfall.

It makes the urgent feel ultimate.
It makes the temporary feel worth more than the eternal.
It whispers, Take it now. Feel it now. Feed it now.
And it never tells you the real price until afterward.

But here’s what we miss: Esau did not lose everything in one dramatic collapse. He lost it because he treated holy things like they were cheap. He despised the blessing before he ever sold it. The stew only exposed what was already in his heart.
And how many people are still doing the same?

Trading purity for pleasure.
Calling for craving.
Peace for a moment of flesh.
Destiny for something that cannot even satisfy by tomorrow.
Brother, sister—be careful what your hunger is teaching you to value.

Not every empty feeling must be fed.
Not every desire deserves a yes.
Not every offer is worth the cost.
But this is where grace walks in.

Because Jesus did what Esau did not. In the wilderness, hungry and weak, Christ was tempted to turn stones into bread. But He refused to surrender eternal obedience for temporary relief. Where Esau failed, Jesus stood. Where we have traded holy things for passing pleasures, Jesus offers mercy, forgiveness, and a new heart.
Your worst trade is not beyond His redemption.

If you have sold peace for sin, come back.
If you have despised what God called precious, repent.
If your appetites have been louder than your calling, run to Christ.

He does not just forgive foolish exchanges.
He restores ruined people.
Don’t sell tomorrow’s blessing for today’s craving.

Choose Christ over appetite.
Choose holiness over impulse.
Choose eternity over the stew.
